collection: NERDC JSS 1 Intermediate Science skill acquisition and science ethics
note: Original structured classroom practice. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain skill acquisition using evidence of increasingly independent performance.
questions.prompt: At first Amina needs help to save her class notes in the correct folder. After practising with feedback, she can save and retrieve a new file by herself. Explain what skill acquisition means and use one detail to show it here.
questions.answer: Skill acquisition is learning how to perform a task through instruction and practice. Amina can now save and retrieve a new file independently.
questions.explanation: Applying the procedure independently to a new file shows that her ability has developed.

markingGuide.description: Explains that skill acquisition involves developing an ability through learning or practice.
Cites evidence of independent performance.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.subtopic: Choosing a skill for a shared need
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a group would learn a skill for decision-making.
questions.prompt: A school club regularly has too few materials for its craft sessions because it buys supplies without checking what is left. Why would learning to keep a stock record help the club decide what to buy?
questions.answer: A stock record shows what is available and what is running low. The club can use that information to buy needed supplies and avoid unnecessary purchases.
questions.explanation: Keeping records helps the club make purchasing decisions from evidence.

markingGuide.description: Explains what a stock record tells the club.
Links that information to a purchasing decision.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain a reason for practising clear communication before an emergency.
questions.prompt: In a school drill, one pupil reports a problem but leaves out the location. Explain why a class should practise giving a clear location when reporting an emergency and say what an informative location could include.
questions.answer: A clear location helps an adult find the right place promptly. A report could include the building name, room number or a familiar landmark.
questions.explanation: Practising clear reports can help people communicate essential information under pressure.

markingGuide.description: Links a clear location to prompt help.
Gives a useful identifying detail.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Identify distinct types of skills used to develop a community display.
questions.prompt: At a school exhibition, one team takes clear pictures of garden produce and another arranges the pictures, headings and descriptions on a printable page. Name the skill used by each team and explain how the tasks differ.
questions.answer: The first team uses photography to capture the images. The second uses desktop publishing or page layout to organise images and text for printing.
questions.explanation: Capturing visual evidence and laying it out for readers are separate parts of making the display.

markingGuide.description: Names photography and describes its role.
Names desktop publishing or page layout and describes its role.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain a practical benefit of acquiring a repair skill.
questions.prompt: A learner acquires the skill of hand-stitching and uses it to mend an open seam on a school bag. Explain one benefit to the household and one benefit related to use of materials.
questions.answer: The household may avoid paying for an immediate replacement. Keeping the bag in service also reduces waste from discarding it early.
questions.explanation: A useful repair skill can extend the life of an item and reduce replacement costs.

markingGuide.description: Explains a plausible household benefit.
Explains a distinct benefit involving waste or material use.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Explain an ethical issue in a science activity.
questions.prompt: A team borrows measuring equipment. One member accidentally damages it and suggests returning it quietly so the team can present its project on time. Identify the ethical issue and propose a responsible action.
questions.answer: The team must decide whether to disclose the damage and take responsibility. It should tell the teacher or owner what happened and ask how to put it right.
questions.explanation: The decision concerns honesty and responsibility to people who own or may later use the equipment.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the ethical issue of disclosure or responsibility.
Proposes reporting the damage to the responsible person.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Choose an observation method that reduces unnecessary disturbance.
questions.prompt: A group wants to record how ants move along a path outside a classroom. One plan blocks the path with tape and another records their movement from a distance. Choose a plan and explain how it respects living things.
questions.answer: Record from a distance. This allows observation without obstructing the ants or changing their route unnecessarily.
questions.explanation: Low-disturbance observation protects the animals and can give a better record of ordinary behaviour.

markingGuide.description: Selects observation from a distance.
Explains a plausible effect of blocking the path or a benefit of minimising disturbance.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Explain an environmental consequence of a technology and a practical mitigation.
questions.prompt: A school installs solar lamps whose batteries can be taken out by a technician when worn out. The purchase plan covers installation only. Identify one environmental concern at the end of battery life and propose one addition to the plan.
questions.answer: Discarded batteries can contribute to pollution if mishandled. Arrange a return through the supplier or an appropriate battery collection programme.
questions.explanation: Planning for worn-out components reduces the risk of improper disposal.

markingGuide.description: Identifies a plausible environmental problem linked to discarded batteries.
Proposes an appropriate collection or return arrangement.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Explain how retaining unexpected results supports honest scientific reporting.
questions.prompt: In two trials a paper bridge holds a stack of washers. In a third trial the bridge collapses much earlier. The group wants to leave out the third result because it spoils the pattern. What should it record, and why?
questions.answer: Record all three results and note any known difference in how the third trial was performed. An unexpected result may reveal variation or a problem worth checking.
questions.explanation: Reporting results with relevant notes lets readers assess the evidence and decide whether more trials are needed.

markingGuide.description: Says to retain and label the unexpected result.
Gives a reason connected to the reliability or transparency of the evidence.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Explain how sensitivity to local practices can improve a design decision.
questions.prompt: A proposed school water point would use the part of a courtyard where community groups meet. What should the design team ask users before choosing the site, and how could the answers affect its decision?
questions.answer: Ask when, where and how the space is used and whether the proposed location would cause problems. The answers could support another layout or location that keeps meeting space available.
questions.explanation: Listening to people who use the site can identify impacts that are invisible on a site drawing.

markingGuide.description: Proposes a relevant consultation question.
Shows one way the answer could change the design decision.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Identify a hazard, possible harm and control before a classroom experiment.
questions.prompt: Before a demonstration, pupils notice that a projector cable runs across the aisle they will use to reach their tables. Identify the hazard and possible harm, then give one control to arrange before the demonstration.
questions.answer: The cable crossing the aisle is a trip hazard. Someone could fall and be injured. Ask the teacher to reroute the cable out of the walkway or secure it with a suitable cable cover.
questions.explanation: A risk check connects the hazard to a possible injury and identifies how to reduce the risk before people are exposed.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the cable across the aisle as the hazard.
States a plausible harm from tripping.
Proposes an appropriate preventive control.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a design team should consider effects on nearby people.
questions.prompt: A community workshop plans to run a loud testing machine late in the evening. Name someone beyond the operators who could be affected and explain how changing the test arrangements could reduce the impact.
questions.answer: Nearby residents could lose sleep because of noise. Scheduling tests earlier or using a suitable quieter enclosure could reduce disturbance.
questions.explanation: Technical work can affect people who receive none of its immediate benefits. Planning can reduce that burden.

markingGuide.description: Identifies an affected group and explains the likely impact.
Suggests a feasible change linked to reduced disturbance.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.topic: Ethical Issues in Science and Development
questions.learningObjective: Identify an unequal effect of a science project and propose a fair response.
questions.prompt: A school introduces a weather station. Only pupils with a smartphone can see its readings. Identify who is excluded and propose a way for them to use the data in class.
questions.answer: Pupils without smartphone access are excluded. Sharing a printout, a classroom chart or access through a school computer would let them use the readings too.
questions.explanation: Making shared data available in more than one way can give learners more equal access to the same project.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the group excluded by phone-only access.
Proposes a realistic way to give that group access.
